title.en: Odudua and the Cradle of Humankind at Ife

region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), chs. 2-4

summary.en: Ellis records the priests' myths of Odudua the Earth-mother, wed to the sky-god Obatala like two shut calabashes of Heaven and Earth; their first children are Land and Water, and the first human couple, Obalofun (Lord of Speech) and Iya (Mother), come out of the goddess at Ife — the cradle of the human race.
summary.zh: 埃利斯錄祭司神話：地母奧都杜瓦與天神奧巴塔拉如兩合之瓢，天地相扣；所生首子即陸與水；首對人類歐巴洛馮（言之主）與伊雅（母）自女神體中出於伊費——人類搖籃之地。

sensitivity.note: Living religious tradition of the Yoruba. Recorded from an 1894 colonial-era collection; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Orisha worshippers.

passages.text: Odudua is the wife of Obatala, but she was coeval with Olorun, and not made by him, as was her husband. Other natives, however, say that she came from Ife, the holy city, in common with most of the other gods, as described in a myth which we shall come to shortly. Odudua represents the earth, married to the anthropomorphic sky-god. Obatala and Odudua, or Heaven and Earth, resemble, say the priests, two large cut-calabashes, which, when once shut, can never be opened. This is symbolised in the temples by two whitened saucer-shaped calabashes, placed one covering the other; the upper one of which represents the concave firmament stretching over and meeting the earth, the lower one, at the horizon.

The second story, which cannot be any older than the myth of Yemaja, of which it is a part, is sufficiently precise to give the name of the first couple, that of the man being Obalofun (Lord of Speech), and that of the woman Iya (Mother). After coming out of the goddess at Ife, they settled there, and had a numerous progeny, which increased and multiplied till the whole earth was populated, hence it is that Ife is considered the cradle of the human race.

title.en: The Destruction of Mankind and the Drunken Hathor
title.zh: 人類之滅與醉酒的哈托爾

region.en: Tomb of Seti I, Thebes, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及底比斯塞提一世陵墓

texts.period: New Kingdom text (tomb of Seti I, c. 1290 BCE); trans. Budge, 1912

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge, 'The Legend of the Destruction of Mankind'

summary.en: Ra, grown old, learns that men murmur against him and sends his Eye as the goddess Hathor to slay the rebels; she wades in their blood and would destroy all mankind, until Ra has 7,000 vessels of beer mixed with mandrakes and blood poured over the land — she drinks, becomes drunk, and mankind is saved.
summary.zh: 太陽神拉年老，聞世人怨謗，遣其目為哈托爾女神誅叛者；女神涉血而行，欲盡滅人類。拉命以曼德拉草與血和酒七千甕傾於田野——女神飲而醉，人類得免於難。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary-religious text of Egypt; presented as a comparative-mythology text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Let thine Eye go forth and let it destroy for thee those who revile thee with words of evil, for there is no eye whatsoever that can go before it and resist thee and it when it journeyeth in the form of Hathor. Thereupon this goddess went forth and slew the men and the women who were on the mountain (or, desert land). And the Majesty of this god said, "Come, come in peace, O Hathor, for the work is accomplished." Then this goddess said, "Thou hast made me to live, for when I gained the mastery over men and women it was sweet to my heart;" and the Majesty of Ra said, "I myself will be master over them as [their] king, and I will destroy them." And it came to pass that Sekhet of the offerings waded about in the night season in their blood, beginning at Suten-henen.

And behold, when the maidservants were bruising the grain for [making] beer, these mandrakes were placed in the vessels which were to hold the beer, and some of the blood of the men and women [who had been slain]. Now they made seven thousand vessels of beer. [...] Then the Majesty of the King of the South and North in the three-fold beauty of the night caused to be poured out these vases of beer which make [men] to lie down (or, sleep), and the meadows of the Four Heavens were filled with beer (or, water) by reason of the Souls of the Majesty of this god. And it came to pass that when this goddess arrived at the dawn of day, she found these [Heavens] flooded [with beer], and she was pleased thereat; and she drank [of the beer and blood], and her heart rejoiced, and she became drunk, and she gave no further attention to men and women.

title.en: Atrahasis: The Clamor of Men and the Plagues
title.zh: 阿特拉哈西斯：人間喧囂與瘟疫

region.zh: 尼普魯（眾神之城，伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE; trans. Rogers, 1912

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, trans. Robert W. Rogers, 'Ea and Atrakhasis'

summary.en: Ellil, troubled by the ceaseless clamor of the teeming men below, holds assembly and sends pestilence to make an end of it; the wise Atrakhasis turns his thought to Ea his lord and pleads for mankind — the Old Babylonian myth that explains why the gods made death and sent the flood.
summary.zh: 眾生滋繁，喧囂不息，恩利爾神擾而集會，降瘟疫以絕其聲；智者阿特拉哈西斯歸念其主埃亞，為人類哀求——此古巴比倫神話釋死亡與洪水之由。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Mesopotamian myth; presented as a comparative-mythology text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: By their clamor he (Ellil) was [troubled] on account of their [...]. [Ellil] held his assembly and said to the gods, his children: "The clamor of men [disturbs me?] Because of their clamor I am troubled." [...] let chill come! [Quickly] let pestilence make an end to their clamor. Like a tempest shall rise against them. Illness, headache, chill, calamity!

[Quickly] did the pestilence make an end to their clamor. Like a tempest rose against them, illness, headache, chill, calamity. The wise Atrakhasis, the man, -- to Ea, his lord, is his thought turned, [he] speaks with his god, his [lord] Ea speaks with him. Atrakhasis opened his mouth, [he spoke to] Ea, his lord: "O lord, [Ea] men are in trouble, thy anger consumes the land. [...] thou who hast created us, let the illness, headache, chills, calamity [cease?]."

title.en: The Bilingual of Creation: Marduk Lays the Reed-Work
title.zh: 雙語創世記：馬爾杜克鋪蘆葦

region.zh: 埃利都與尼普魯（蘇美，伊拉克）

texts.period: Sumerian/Akkadian bilingual text (recorded c. 1000 BCE); trans. Rogers, 1912

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, trans. Robert W. Rogers, 'Another Version of the Creation of the World by Marduk (Bilingual of Creation)'

summary.en: A Sumerian-and-Akkadian creation text: before Eridu, Nippur, or any city was built, all lands were sea; Marduk laid a reed-work on the face of the waters, formed dust upon it, made mankind, the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, the cattle and beasts, and built the holy cities in their place.
summary.zh: 蘇美—阿卡德雙語創世文書：埃利都、尼普魯諸城未建之先，大地皆海；馬爾杜克於水面鋪蘆葦之基，揚塵其上，造人類、底格里斯與幼發拉底二河、牛獸百物，並建眾神聖城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Sumerian-Babylonian liturgical creation text; presented as a comparative-mythology text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The holy house, the house of the gods, in the holy place had not yet been made; No reed had sprung up, no tree had been created. No brick had been laid, no mould had been fashioned, No house had been made, no city had been built; No city had been made, no creature had been established. Nippur had not been made, E-kur had not been built; Erech had not been made, E-ana had not been built; The Deep had not been made, Eridu had not been built; [...] All lands were sea. When the middle of the sea was a water basin; In those days Eridu was made, E-sagil was built, E-sagil, where in the midst of the deep the god Lugal-dul-azaga dwelt, Babylon was made, and E-sagil was finished, The gods, the Anunaki, he made at one time; The holy city, the dwelling of the heart's desire, they proclaimed supreme.

Marduk laid a reed-work upon the face of the waters, He formed dust and poured it out upon the reed-work. To cause the gods to dwell in a habitation of their heart's desire, He formed mankind. The goddess Aruru, with him, created the seed of mankind. The beasts of the field and living things in the field he created. He created the Tigris and the Euphrates, and set them in their place, Their names he did well declare. The grass, the rush of the marsh, the reed, and the forest he created.

title.en: The Creation of Cattle and Beasts

region.en: Nippur, Sumer (found in Nineveh library), Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（蘇美；見尼尼微圖書館藏板），伊拉克

texts.period: Mesopotamian creation-series fragment (Assyrian library copy); trans. Rogers, 1912

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, trans. Robert W. Rogers, 'The Creation of Cattle and Beasts'

summary.en: A fragment of the Mesopotamian creation-series tradition: when the gods in assembly had made the heavens, formed the firmament and settled the earth, bringing living things of all kinds to life and dividing the wild beasts from the creatures of the city, Nin-igi-azag created two small creatures, one white and one black, in the assembly of the beasts.
summary.zh: 美索不達米亞創世系列殘板：眾神集會造天、成穹、定地，賦萬物以生，分野獸與城居之屬；尼尼吉阿札格於獸群之中造二小獸，一白一黑。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Mesopotamian creation fragment; presented as a comparative-mythology text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When the gods in their assembly had made the [heavens] Had formed the firmament, and settled the [earth], living things [of all kinds] had brought into life, And had made the cattle of the field, and the beasts of the field, and the moving things of the city [...] [And between the beasts] of the field and the moving things of the city had divided [...] Then arose (?) Nin-igi-azag and [created] two small creatures [In the] assembly of the beasts he made their [form] beautiful [...] one white [and one black...]

title.en: Llew and the Woman Made of Flowers

region.zh: 威爾斯斯諾登山／丁勒堡

texts.period: Mabinogion, 'Math son of Mathonwy', 13th c. MS; trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, 'Math the son of Mathonwy'

summary.en: Arianrod curses her son Llew never to have a wife of any race on earth; so Math and Gwydion form a woman out of the blossoms of the oak, the broom, and the meadow-sweet. When Gronw's poisoned dart fells Llew, he flies up as an eagle, until Gwydion sings him down from the oak and strikes him with his wand.
summary.zh: 阿里安羅德咒其子勒烏永不得世上任何族類之妻；馬斯與格威狄恩遂以橡花、金雀花與繡線菊花合成一女，名曰布洛代薇德。格隆之毒鏢傷勒烏，勒烏化鷹棲橡樹；格威狄恩詠歌三闋召之，以魔杖擊之復其人形。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Welsh mythic literature (Insular Celtic cycle); presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: They went thereupon unto Math the son of Mathonwy, and complained unto him most bitterly of Arianrod. Gwydion showed him also how he had procured arms for the youth. 'Well,' said Math, 'we will seek, I and thou, by charms and illusion, to form a wife for him out of flowers. He has now come to man's stature, and he is the comeliest youth that was ever beheld.' So they took the blossoms of the oak, and the blossoms of the broom, and the blossoms of the meadow-sweet, and produced from them a maiden, the fairest and most graceful that man ever saw. And they baptized her, and gave her the name of Blodeuwedd.

Thereupon Gronw rose up from the bill which is called Bryn Kyvergyr, and he rested on one knee, and flung the poisoned dart and struck him on the side, so that the shaft started out, but the head of the dart remained in. Then he flew up in the form of an eagle and gave a fearful scream. And thenceforth was he no more seen.

And Gwydion came under the tree, and looked what it might be that the sow was feeding on. And he saw that she was eating putrid flesh and vermin. Then looked he up to the top of the tree, and as he looked he beheld on the top of the tree an eagle, and when the eagle shook itself, there fell vermin and putrid flesh from off it, and these the sow devoured. And it seemed to him that the eagle was Llew. [...] And the eagle came down upon Gwydion's knee. And Gwydion struck him with his magic wand, so that he returned to his own form. No one ever saw a more piteous sight, for he was nothing but skin and bone.

title.en: Vari, the Very Beginning, and Vatea

region.zh: 庫克群島曼加伊亞

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), 'The Beginning of all Things'

summary.en: In Mangaian chant the universe is the hollow of a vast cocoa-nut shell; at its narrow bottom lives Vari-ma-te-takere, The-very-beginning, who plucked off bits of her own sides to make the first gods — Vatea, half man and half fish, father of gods and men, whose one eye is the sun and the other the moon.
summary.zh: 曼加伊亞創世歌：宇宙如巨大椰殼之腔；其最底處居「太初」瓦里馬特泰克雷，自體側摘片造諸神——首生瓦泰亞，半人半魚，為神人之父；其一目為日，一目為月。

sensitivity.note: Polynesian oral tradition recorded from the last priests of Mangaia; presented as an archival record of a faith no longer practised in its traditional form.

passages.text: In the lowest depth of Avaiki, where the sides of the imaginary shell nearly meet, lives a woman -- a demon, of flesh and blood -- named Vari-ma-te-takere, or The-very-beginning. Such is the narrowness of her territory that her knees and chin touch, no other position being possible. Vari-ma-te-takere was very anxious for progeny. One day she plucked off a bit of her right side, and it became a human being -- the first man Avatea, or Vatea [...] Now Vatea, the father of gods and men, was half man and half fish, the division being like the two halves of the human body. [...] Thus one eye of Vatea was human, the other a fish-eye.

On another occasion Vari-ma-te-takere tore off a second bit from that same right side, and it became Tinirau, or In-numerable, who, like his brother, had a second and fishy form. [...] Another day Vari-ma-te-takere took a bit off her left side, and it became Tango, or Support, who went to live at Enua-Kura, or The-land-of-red-parrot-feathers. A fourth child was produced from a bit of the same left side, and was named Tumuteanaoa, or Echo [...] A fifth child originated from a bit of that same left side of the Great Mother, and was designated Raka, or Trouble, who presides, like Aeolus, over the winds.

title.en: Maui Makes the Sun Captive

region.zh: 庫克群島曼加伊亞

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), 'The sun made captive'

summary.en: The days are too short for any work or incantation to be finished; so the redoubtable Maui resolves to capture the Sun-god Ra and compel him to obey the dictates of his conqueror — snaring the god by the neck with a rope and forcing him to move more reasonably across the sky.
summary.zh: 白晝苦短，諸業未成日已沒；無畏之毛伊遂謀縛太陽神拉，以繩套神之頸，迫其緩行——自此日月運行有度。

sensitivity.note: Polynesian oral tradition recorded from the last priests of Mangaia; presented as an archival record of a faith no longer practised in its traditional form.

passages.text: Maui had secured fire for the advantage of mortals, had elevated the sky; but there remained one great evil to be remedied -- the sun had a trick of setting every now and then, so that it was impossible to get through any work. Even an oven of food could not be prepared and cooked before the sun had set. Nor could a "karakia," or incantation to the gods, be chanted through ere they were overtaken by darkness. Maui resolved to remove this great evil. Now Ra, or the Sun, is a living creature and divine; in form resembling a man, and possessed of fearful energy. His golden locks are displayed morning and evening to mankind. [...] But the redoubtable Maui was not to be discouraged. He resolved to capture the Sun-god Ra, and compel him to obey the dictates of his conqueror.

title.en: Ina, the Fairy Voyager

region.zh: 庫克群島曼加伊亞

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), 'Ina, the fairy voyager'

summary.en: The girl Ina rides a shark across the ocean to the Sacred Isle, piercing her cocoa-nut for water on the creature's erected dorsal fin — and cracking it on its forehead, which is why sharks bear 'Ina's bump' to this day; the shark-king Tekea the Great carries her past her enemies to the long-sought shore.
summary.zh: 少女伊娜乘鯊渡海往聖島；以椰子承鯊立起之背鰭取水，又於鯊額擊破椰殼——故鯊額至今有「伊娜之凸」；鯊王特克亞大神護其過敵鯊之群，達於久覓之岸。

sensitivity.note: Polynesian oral tradition recorded from the last priests of Mangaia; presented as an archival record of a faith no longer practised in its traditional form.

passages.text: At the margin of the ocean a shark came in sight. Addressing the shark in words very like those formerly used, to her great delight the huge fish came to her feet, and Ina mounted triumphantly on its broad back, carrying in her hand two cocoa-nuts to eat. When halfway on the dangerous voyage to the Sacred Isle, Ina felt very thirsty, and told the shark so. The obedient fish immediately erected its dorsal fin, on which Ina pierced the eye of one of her nuts. [...] The shark, smarting from the blow, dived into the depths of the ocean, leaving the girl to float as best she could. From that day there has been a marked protuberance on the forehead of all sharks, called "Ina's bump."

title.en: Qat Makes Things, and Buys the Night

region.zh: 萬那杜班克斯群島莫塔島

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (1891), ch. 10

summary.en: Qat of the Banks Islands begins to make things — men, pigs, trees, rocks — then sails to the foot of the sky to buy the night from Night herself; his brothers see the sun sink for the first time, fear that they shall die, and are taught to sleep till Qat cuts the night open with a piece of red obsidian.
summary.zh: 班克斯群島之神卡特造人、豬、樹、石；復航至天之腳下，向黑夜女神購得夜。弟眾初見日落，驚懼呼死；卡特教其瞑目而眠，至時以赤曜石割開黑夜，曙光復現。

sensitivity.note: Melanesian oral tradition recorded from native teachers of the Banks Islands; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Melanesian communities.

passages.text: There Qat began to make things, men, pigs, trees, rocks, as the fancy took him. But when he had made all sorts of things he still knew not how to make night, and the daytime was always light. [...] Then, seeking what he could do with the daylight, he heard that there was night at Vava, in the Torres Islands; so he took a pig and tied it, and put it into his canoe, and sailed over to Vava, where he bought night, qong, from I Qong, Night, who lived there. [...] Then he let go the night.

'What is this coming out of the sea,' they cried, 'and covering the sky?' 'That is night,' said he; 'sit down on both sides of the house, and when you feel something in your eyes, lie down and be quiet.' Presently it was dark, and their eyes began to blink. 'Qat! Qat! what is this? shall we die?' 'Shut your eyes,' said he; 'this is it, go to sleep.' When night had lasted long enough the cock began to crow and the birds to twitter; Qat took a piece of red obsidian and cut the night with it; the light over which the night had spread itself shone forth again, and Qat's brothers awoke.

According to the story as told in Mota, Qat made men and pigs at first in the same form, but on his brothers remonstrating with him on the sameness of his creatures, he beat down the pigs to go on all fours and made men walk upright. Man was made of clay, the red clay from the marshy riverside at Vanua Lava.

title.en: Qat, Marawa the Spider, and the Canoes
title.zh: 卡特、蜘蛛馬拉瓦與獨木舟

region.zh: 萬那杜班克斯群島莫塔島

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (1891), ch. 10

summary.en: Qat cuts a great tree for a canoe, but every night his secret work is undone — until he catches the little old man Marawa, the spider, replacing the chips; Marawa promises to finish the canoe with his nails, and the brothers' own canoes, launched in envy, sink one by one.
summary.zh: 卡特伐大樹造舟，然夜夜其功盡毀——樹身復合如初；伏而擒之，乃小老翁蜘蛛馬拉瓦。馬拉瓦諾以指爪為之成舟；弟眾嫉而自造之舟，下水一一沈沒。

sensitivity.note: Melanesian oral tradition recorded from native teachers of the Banks Islands; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Melanesian communities.

passages.text: Qat cut down a large tree well suited for a canoe, and worked secretly every day, but made no progress in his work; every day when he returned to work he found the wood that he had chopped away replaced, and the tree made solid again. [...] Presently he saw a little old man with long white hair creep out of the ground and begin to replace the chips, each in the place from which it had been cut, till the tree trunk was almost whole again. [...] But Marawa, the spider, another very powerful vui, for this was he, entreated Qat, 'Ah, friend, don't kill me, and I will make your canoe all right again;' and he worked at it, and soon finished it with his nails. When all the canoes were finished, Qat bade his brothers launch their own, and as each was launched he lifted his hand, and one by one they sank.

title.en: How Tagaro Made the Sea

region.zh: 萬那杜新赫布里底群島奧羅拉島

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (1891), ch. 19 'How Tagaro made the Sea'

summary.en: In old times the sea was only a small pool behind Tagaro's house, walled in with stone; his two sons, forbidden to go there, breach the wall playing at fish — and the water runs out with a roar, spreading into the great sea, while the old woman who tried to stop it turns to stone.
summary.zh: 太古之海，僅塔加羅屋後小池，石牆圍之。其二子犯禁戲魚，推石決牆——水轟然而出，遂成大海；老嫗以身當之，化為石，今猶在焉。

sensitivity.note: Melanesian oral tradition recorded from native teachers of the New Hebrides; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Melanesian communities.

passages.text: They say that he made the sea, and that in old times the sea was quite small, like a common pool upon the beach, and that this pool was at the back of his house, and that there were fish in the pool, and that he had built a stone wall round it. [...] So when he was gone the thought entered into the mind of those two, Why has our father forbidden us to go there? [...] And one of the boys stood on the stones Tagaro had built up, and he sees the fish, and he shoots at one and hits it; and as he runs to catch hold of it he threw down a stone, and then the water ran out. [...] and the sea followed as it flowed. And they think that the old woman turned into a stone, and lies now on the part of Maewo near Raga.

title.en: Lumawig Makes the People of the Reeds

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Creation'

summary.en: In the beginning there were no people on the earth; Lumawig the Great Spirit came down from the sky, cut many reeds, and set them in pairs throughout the world — commanding them to speak, and each pair became a man and a woman whose language differed from every other couple's.
summary.zh: 太初大地無人；大神盧馬維格自天而下，刈蘆葦甚多，分置世界各地為偶，命之曰言——蘆葦即化為人，每地一男一女，其語各異。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities.

passages.text: In the beginning there were no people on the earth. Lumawig, the Great Spirit, came down from the sky and cut many reeds. He divided these into pairs which he placed in different parts of the world, and then he said to them, "You must speak." Immediately the reeds became people, and in each place was a man and a woman who could talk, but the language of each couple differed from that of the others. Then Lumawig commanded each man and woman to marry, which they did. By and by there were many children, all speaking the same language as their parents. These, in turn, married and had many children. In this way there came to be many people on the earth.

title.en: Lumawig's Sons and the Flood

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省波基斯

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Flood Story'

summary.en: Lumawig's sons flood the flat world to raise mountains, drowning all the people but one brother and sister on the peak of Pokis; Lumawig builds a great fire to warm the two survivors, the waters dry away, and the brother and sister marry to re-people the earth.
summary.zh: 盧馬維格二子引水漫淹平坦之世以起群山，世人盡溺，唯波基斯山巔兄妹二人得存；盧馬維格燃巨火暖之，洪水退去，兄妹成婚，人類繁衍復興。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities.

passages.text: "Let us cause water to flow over all the world and cover it, and then mountains will rise up." So they caused water to flow over all the earth, and when it was covered they took the head-basket of the town and set it for a trap. [...] Now Lumawig looked down from his place in the sky and saw that his sons had flooded the earth and that in all the world there was just one spot which was not covered. And he saw that all the people in the world had been drowned except one brother and sister who lived in Pokis. [...] As soon as Lumawig reached Pokis he built a big fire which warmed the brother and sister; and the water evaporated so that the world was as it was before, except that now there were mountains. The brother and sister married and had children, and thus there came to be many people on the earth.

title.en: Melu Makes the Earth and the First People

region.en: Lake Sebu region, South Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨南哥達巴托省賽布湖

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan: 'The Story of the Creation'

summary.en: The giant Melu shapes the world out of his own rubbed-off dead skin, then fashions two men from the leftovers; Tau Tana interferes and sets their noses upside down, and Melu, whipping the forms until they moved, later saves their hair and dry skin to make companions — hence the many people of the earth.
summary.zh: 巨人梅盧搓自身蛻下之死皮而成大地，復以餘料塑二人；塔烏塔納從地底來擾，將鼻捏反。梅盧鞭打土偶使其行動，又貯其髮膚，造為新伴——世上人類由是繁盛。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bilaan narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bilaan communities.

passages.text: Finally Melu decided to make the earth; so he worked very hard in putting the dead skin into shape, and when it was finished he was so pleased with it that he determined to make two beings like himself, though smaller, to live on it. Taking the remnants of the material left after making the earth he fashioned two men but just as they were all finished except their noses, Tau Tana from below the earth appeared and wanted to help him. Melu did not wish any assistance, and a great argument ensued. Tau Tana finally won his point and made the noses which he placed on the people upside down. When all was finished, Melu and Tau Tana whipped the forms until they moved.

The people were very grateful to him, and promised to do anything he should ask of them. Before he left for the sky, they told him that they were very unhappy living on the great earth all alone, so he told them to save all the hair from their heads and the dry skin from their bodies and the next time he came he would make them some companions. And in this way there came to be a great many people on the earth.

title.en: Viracocha Creates the World at Tiahuanacu
title.zh: 維拉科查於蒂亞瓦納科創世

region.zh: 蒂亞瓦納科（科利亞蘇尤，玻利維亞／秘魯）

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham, 1907

source.work: Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, chs. 6-7 (Hakluyt Society, trans. Sir Clements Markham)

summary.en: In the beginning Viracocha created a dark world without sun, moon, or stars, and a race of giants; after the flood called uno pachacuti, 'water that overturns the land,' he created the sun, moon, and stars on the island of Titicaca, and at Tiahuanacu sculptured on stone all the nations he meant to create — calling them forth from lakes, caves, trees, and rocks.
summary.zh: 太初維拉科查造暗黑之世，無日月星辰，又造巨人之屬；洪水「翻地之水」過後，遂於的的喀喀島造日月眾星，復於蒂亞瓦納科以石雕萬族之形——呼其名而諸族自湖、泉、洞、樹、石中湧出，遍居大地。

sensitivity.note: Inca tradition recorded under Viceroy Toledo's commission from sworn Inca witnesses; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically.

passages.text: The natives of this land affirm that in the beginning, and before this world was created, there was a being called Viracocha. He created a dark world without sun, moon or stars. Owing to this creation he was named Viracocha Pachayachachi, which means "Creator of all things." And when he had created the world he formed a race of giants of disproportioned greatness [...] He then created men in his likeness as they are now; and they lived in darkness.

The flood being passed and the land dry, Viracocha determined to people it a second time, and, to make it more perfect, he decided upon creating luminaries to give it light. With this object he went, with his servants, to a great lake in the Collao, in which there is an island called Titicaca [...] Viracocha went to this island, and presently ordered that the sun, moon, and stars should come forth, and be set in the heavens to give light to the world, and it was so.

He went to a place now called Tiahuanacu in the province of Colla-suyu, and in this place he sculptured and designed on a great piece of stone, all the nations that he intended to create. [...] His servants, obeying the command of Viracocha, set out on their journey and work. [...] At the sound of his voice every place obeyed, and people came forth, some from lakes, others from fountains, valleys, caves, trees, rocks and hills, spreading over the land and multiplying to form the nations which are to-day in Peru.

title.en: The Children of the Window of Production

region.zh: 秘魯庫斯科近郊帕卡里坦普

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham, 1907

source.work: Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 11 (Hakluyt Society, trans. Sir Clements Markham)

summary.en: Six leagues from Cuzco is the hill Tampu-tocco, 'the house of windows,' where three windows open in the rock; from the rich window Ccapac-tocco came forth four brothers and four sisters, created and sent by Ticci Viracocha to be lords — among them Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo, the founders of the Inca line.
summary.zh: 庫斯科六里外有山名坦普托科，「窗之屋」，岩上開三窗；四男四女自其中之富窗「卡帕克托科」而出，乃蒂奇維拉科查所造所遣之主——印加王朝之祖曼科卡帕克與瑪瑪奧克洛即在焉。

sensitivity.note: Inca tradition recorded under Viceroy Toledo's commission from sworn Inca witnesses; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically.

passages.text: All the native Indians of this land relate and affirm that the Incas Ccapac originated in this way. Six leagues S.S.W. of Cuzco by the road which the Incas made, there is a place called Paccari-tampu, which means 'the house of production,' at which there is a hill called Tampu-tocco, meaning 'the house of windows.' It is certain that in this hill there are three windows [...] From the chief window of 'Ccapac-tocco,' came four men and four women, called brethren. These knew no father nor mother, beyond the story they told that they were created and came out of the said window by order of Ticci Viracocha, and they declared that Viracocha created them to be lords. For this reason they took the name of Inca, which is the same as lord.

title.en: The Giants of the First Making

region.zh: 的的喀喀湖（玻利維亞／秘魯）

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham, 1907

source.work: Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7 (Hakluyt Society, trans. Sir Clements Markham)

summary.en: A variant told by the old people: at the Titicaca site Viracocha first formed shapes of large strong men out of proportion, then remade them of his own stature and gave them life; thence they set out to people the land — the memory, in Inca tradition, of the builders of Tiahuanacu.
summary.zh: 古人所傳異說：維拉科查初於的的喀喀之地塑壯偉巨人，以其失度，遂改塑如己身之度而賦以生；諸人由是四出而居——印加傳統以此記蒂亞瓦納科建城古族之由來。

sensitivity.note: Inca tradition recorded under Viceroy Toledo's commission from sworn Inca witnesses; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically.

passages.text: Others affirm that this creation of Viracocha was made from the Titicaca site where, having originally formed some shapes of large strong men which seemed to him out of proportion, he made them again of his stature which was, as they say, the average height of men, and being made he gave them life. Thence they set out to people the land.

title.en: Makonaima and the Wondrous Tree

region.zh: 蓋亞那埃斯塞基博盆地阿卡瓦奧之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, The Indian Tribes of Guiana (1868), ch. 10 'Mythology and Legendary Tales'

summary.en: In the beginning Makonaima, the great spirit whom no man hath seen, created the birds and beasts with the gift of speech, and set his son Sigu to rule them; then, to surprise his creatures, he caused a wondrous tree to spring from the earth bearing every cultivated fruit — the original stock of all the plants of mankind.
summary.zh: 太初，無人得見之大神馬科納伊瑪造飛禽走獸，皆賦以言，命其子西古統之；又使神樹自地湧出，枝結百果，根生木薯玉蜀黍——世間一切栽培植物之源也。

sensitivity.note: Indigenous Amazonian oral tradition recorded by a missionary in 1868; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically, not as permission to speak for Indigenous communities.

passages.text: In the beginning of this world the birds and beasts were created by Makonaima, -- the great spirit whom no man hath seen. They, at that time, were all endowed with the gift of speech. Sigu, the son of Makonaima, was placed to rule over them. All lived in harmony together and submitted to his gentle dominion. [...] But Makonaima, to surprise his creatures with his bounty, was causing to spring out of the earth an enormous and wonderful tree. Each branch of that great tree produced a different kind of fruit; while from and around its trunk grew bananas, plantains, and cassava; with maize, and corn of all kinds. [...] which (though white men do not know it) is the original stock from whence have sprung all the plants now cultivated among the nations of the earth.

the Great Spirit, having created the heavens and the earth, seated Himself on a huge silk-cotton tree by a river side, and cut off pieces of its bark or wood, which he cast all around. Those which touched the water became fishes; others flew in the air as birds; while some, as animals of various kinds, and lastly man, moved on the earth.

title.en: Aiomun Kondi and the Two Destructions
title.zh: 艾奧蒙孔迪與兩度滅世

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, The Indian Tribes of Guiana (1868), ch. 10 'Mythology and Legendary Tales'

summary.en: The Arawaks tell that the world has twice been destroyed for the evil doings of men — first by fire, then by flood — each time foretold by Aiomun Kondi, the great Dweller on High; the pious Marerewana saved his family in a canoe tied by a long bush-rope to a tree, and found himself not far from home when the waters fell.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人言：世界因人之惡而兩度遭滅——先以火，後以水，皆艾奧蒙孔迪大神預警；虔智之酋馬雷瓦納以長藤繫舟於樹，攜家避洪，水退而故土不遠。

sensitivity.note: Indigenous Amazonian oral tradition recorded by a missionary in 1868; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically, not as permission to speak for Indigenous communities.

passages.text: They also believe that, since the Creation, the world has been twice destroyed; first, by a flame of fire sent to sweep over it, and afterwards by a flood of water. Each of those destructions was on account of the evil doings of men, and specially threatened by Aiomun Kondi, the great "Dweller on High." [...] When the great waters were about to be sent, a chief of distinguished piety and wisdom, named Marerewana, was informed of the coming flood, and saved himself and his family in a large canoe. Being desirous not to drift over the ocean, or far from the home of his fathers, he had prepared a cable of 'bush-rope' of great length, and with it he tied his bark to the trunk of a large tree. When the waters subsided, he found himself not far from his former abode.

title.en: The Waraus Descend from Above the Sky

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河

source.work: W. H. Brett, The Indian Tribes of Guiana (1868), ch. 10 'Mythology and Legendary Tales'

summary.en: The original home of the Waraus was not this lower world but a pleasant region above the sky; the hunter Okonorote found a hole in the heavens, made a rope of cotton, and led his people down to the game-rich earth — but the last, a stout woman, stuck fast in the aperture, closing the way home forever.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人故鄉不在下界，而在天上樂土；獵人奧科諾羅特獵禽而得天窿，搓棉為繩引族人下界狩獵——末行之肥婦困於穴口，歸路遂絕，瓦勞人自此永居人間。

sensitivity.note: Indigenous Amazonian oral tradition recorded by a missionary in 1868; presented as an archival record — a colonial source to be read critically, not as permission to speak for Indigenous communities.

passages.text: the original abode of the Waraus was not on this lower earth at all, but in a pleasant region above the sky. [...] One of these, named Okonorote, having wandered far in pursuit of a choice bird, discharged an arrow at it, which missed its mark and disappeared. While searching for the arrow he found a hole through which it had fallen, and on looking through it he saw this lower world stretched out beneath [...] They accordingly descended by the same means, followed by their children and their wives, all except the last, -- an unfortunate person who, being too stout to squeeze through, remained fixed in the narrow aperture, completely filling it. [...] The Waraus were thus of necessity confined to this earth, without even a glimpse of their former abode!

title.en: Zohak and the Serpents Fed on Men's Brains

region.zh: 巴比倫（佐哈克之國）／厄爾布爾士山（伊朗）

texts.period: Shah Nameh of Firdausi, c. 1010 CE; trans. and abridged James Atkinson, 1832

source.work: The Shah Nameh of the Persian Poet Firdausi, trans. James Atkinson (Routledge, 1892), 'Zohak'

summary.en: The evil spirit Iblis, in disguise, begs to kiss the young king Zohak's shoulder — and from the kiss spring two black serpents that can only be kept from devouring him by being fed daily with the brains of men; thus the serpent-king's tyranny over Iran begins, until Feridun rises against him.
summary.zh: 惡靈易卜劣廝喬裝乞吻少王佐哈克之肩——吻處湧出雙黑蛇，日飼人腦方免噬主；蛇王虐政由此始，直至費里敦起而伐之。

sensitivity.note: Persian epic literature (Kayanian and legendary cycle); presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: Iblis then kissed the part with fiendish glee, And vanished in an instant. From the touch Sprang two black serpents! Then a tumult rose Among the people, searching for Iblis Through all the palace, but they sought in vain. [...] The serpents writhed about as seeking food. And learned men to see the wonder came, And sage magicians tried to charm away That dreadful evil, but no cure was found.

Iblis again roused him by saying, that if the serpents were fed daily with human brains, which would probably kill them, his life might be prolonged, and made easy. If life has any charm for thee, The brain of man their food must be!

title.en: Zal on Mount Alberz, Nursed by the Simurgh

region.zh: 厄爾布爾士山（伊朗）

texts.period: Shah Nameh of Firdausi, c. 1010 CE; trans. and abridged James Atkinson, 1832

source.work: The Shah Nameh of the Persian Poet Firdausi, trans. James Atkinson (Routledge, 1892), 'The birth of Zal'

summary.en: The infant Zal, born with white hair, is abandoned by his father Sam on mount Alberz — the abode of the Simurgh, the wise wonder-bird, who hears a voice from heaven, takes the crying child up to her nest, and rears him with her young; from his loins, she is told, will spring the champion of the world.
summary.zh: 查爾生而髮白，其父薩姆棄之於厄爾布爾士山——神鳥西摩爾格之居。鳥聞天音，憫而攜啼嬰歸巢，與雛同哺；天音預言其裔將出「世界之雄」。

sensitivity.note: Persian epic literature (Kayanian and legendary cycle); presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: When Sam was made acquainted with these reproaches and taunts of the people, he determined, though with a sorrowful heart, to take him up to the mountain Alberz, and abandon him there to be destroyed by beasts of prey. Alberz was the abode of the Simurgh or Griffin, and, whilst flying about in search of food for his hungry young ones, that surprising animal discovered the child lying alone upon the hard rock, crying and sucking its fingers. The Simurgh, however, felt no inclination to devour him, but compassionately took him up in the air, and conveyed him to his own habitation. [...] The young ones were also kind and affectionate to the infant, which was thus nourished and protected by the Simurgh for several years.

A voice, not earthly, thus addressed The Simurgh in his mountain nest -- "To thee this mortal I resign, Protected by the power divine; Let him thy fostering kindness share, Nourish him with paternal care; For from his loins, in time, will spring The champion of the world, and bring Honour on earth, and to thy name; The heir of everlasting fame."

title.en: Rustem Slays His Son Sohrab

region.zh: 波斯與突朗邊境（布哈拉一帶）

texts.period: Shah Nameh of Firdausi, c. 1010 CE; trans. and abridged James Atkinson, 1832

source.work: The Shah Nameh of the Persian Poet Firdausi, trans. James Atkinson (Routledge, 1892), 'The story of Sohrab'

summary.en: Father and son meet in single combat, neither knowing the other; Rustem hurls the youthful Sohrab to the ground and gives the deadly thrust — then learns, by the royal bracelet his mother gave him as a token, that he has slain his own son: 'My son, my son is slain.'
summary.zh: 父子相逢於陣前而不相識；羅斯坦擲倒少年蘇拉布，予之以致命一擊——旋見其臂上母贈之御鐲為記，方知所殺乃己子：「吾子！吾子亡矣！」

sensitivity.note: Persian epic literature (Kayanian and legendary cycle); presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: With rage convulsive Rustem grasps him round; Bends his strong back, and hurls him to the ground; [...] Like lightning quick he gives the deadly thrust, And spurns the Stripling weltering in the dust. [...] An icy horror chills the Champion's heart, His brain whirls round with agonizing smart [...] Believed at length, with frenzied look, he cries: "Prove thou art mine, confirm my doubting eyes! For I am Rustem!" [...] The loosened mail unfolds the bracelet bright, Unhappy gift! to Rustem's wildered sight; Prostrate he falls -- "By my unnatural hand, My son, my son is slain -- and from the land Uprooted."

[...] By my unnatural hand, My son, my son is slain -- and from the land Uprooted. Frantic, in the dust his hair He rends in agony and deep despair. The Champion rose, but ere he reached the throne, Sohrab had breathed the last expiring groan.

title.en: King Mandhatar, Born from the Crown of the Head

region.zh: 迦濕彌羅經藏所載（象徵位置：拉薩）

source.work: Tibetan Tales derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. Anton von Schiefner, done into English by W. R. S. Ralston (1906), 'King Mandhatar'

summary.en: From the Tibetan Kah-gyur: King Utposhadha's soft crown-tumour breaks open and out comes a golden boy perfect in the thirty-two signs of a Great Being, nursed by eighty thousand queens — Mandhatar, who one day, with his thousand sons and a mighty army, simply rises heavenward and betakes himself to the other continents.
summary.zh: 藏文甘珠爾所傳：鄔波濟瑟吒王頂髻軟瘤既熟而裂，湧出金膚童子，具大人三十二相，八萬后妃乳養之——是為曼陀多王；後一日率千子大軍凌空而起，往赴他洲。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist narrative preserved in the Tibetan canon (Kah-gyur); presented as a mythic corpus text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In olden days, when the life of man was of unlimited duration, lived King Utposhadha. On the crown of his head grew a very soft tumour, somewhat resembling a cushion of cotton or wool, without doing him any harm. When it had become quite ripe and had broken, there came forth from it a boy, shapely and handsome and gracious, perfect in every limb and joint, with a skin the colour of gold, a head like a canopy, long arms, a broad forehead, interlacing eyebrows, and a body provided with the thirty-two signs of a Mahapurusha. Immediately after his birth he was taken into the apartments of the women; and when King Utposhadha's eighty thousand wives saw him, milk began to flow from their breasts, and each of the women cried out, "Let him suck me! let him suck me!" Wherefore he received the name of Mandhatar.

Scarcely had the king entertained this idea when, surrounded by his thousand sons, and accompanied by an army eighteen koti strong, he rose heavenward and betook himself to Purvavidehadvipa, where the four great kings came out to meet him, and the inhabitants of that continent submitted at the mere sight of his host; and when the Asuras afterwards resisted him in battle he conquered them in their own sky-citadel, and lived at ease among the gods.

the seven treasures were revealed, namely, the treasure of the wheel, the treasure of the elephant, the treasure of the horse, the treasure of the gem, the treasure of the wife, the treasure of the householder, and, as the seventh, the treasure of the minister.

title.en: The Magician's Pupil

region.zh: 香醉山（象徵位置：喜馬拉雅）

source.work: Tibetan Tales derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. Anton von Schiefner, done into English by W. R. S. Ralston (1906), 'The Magician's Pupil'

summary.en: A Chandala versed in the Gandhara-Mantra teaches a conceited Brahman youth his spell; the pupil at once soars by magic to the Gandhamadana mountain and plucks out-of-season fruit to amaze the king — and, through his ingratitude, his magic power deserts him.
summary.zh: 旃荼羅術師以乾達婆咒語授傲慢婆羅門少年；其徒旋以術凌空至香醉山，摘非時之果以炫於王——因忘恩負義，術力遂失。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist narrative preserved in the Tibetan canon (Kah-gyur); presented as a mythic corpus text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: As Brahmans are of a conceited nature, the youth could not restrain himself, but must needs immediately make a trial of his magic art on the spot, and then depart. So he employed his magic power, and soared into the sky. When he came to Gandhamadana, he there plucked fruits and flowers which were out of season on earth, and gave them to the king's purohita, who gave them to King Brahmadatta. The king asked where he had got them [...] But in consequence of the youth's ingratitude his magic power deserted him.

a Chandala of Varanasi, versed in spells and magic lore, who, employing the Gandhara-Mantra, was wont to obtain by spells from the Gandhamadana mountain such fruits and flowers as were not in season, and to present them to king Brahmadatta, who made him presents; and it was with him that the Brahman youth served twelve years, propping the drunk master’s bed with his back all night, before the magic lore was communicated to him.

title.en: The Wishing-Trees of Uttarakuru

region.zh: 北俱盧洲（神話北方大陸）

source.work: Tibetan Tales derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. Anton von Schiefner, done into English by W. R. S. Ralston (1906), 'King Mandhatar'

summary.en: Crossing the worlds with his magic gem, King Mandhatar comes to Uttarakuru, whose inhabitants need neither plough nor sow: from the wishing-trees they gather rice un Planted and clothe themselves in garments that grow ready upon the boughs.
summary.zh: 曼陀多王攜神寶遊歷諸界，至北俱盧洲；其人不耕不種：如意樹自生稻米，枝頭自垂衣裳，取之而已。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist narrative preserved in the Tibetan canon (Kah-gyur); presented as a mythic corpus text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: garland-like trees of various colours planted on one side of Sumeru. Having remarked them, he asked the Yaksha Divaukasa what were these garland-like trees of various colours. "O king, these are the wishing-trees of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. The inhabitants of Uttarakuru clothe themselves with garments from the wishing-trees." [...] "O chieftains, those are the wishing-trees that bear the garments with which the inhabitants of Uttarakuru clothe themselves. Ye also, when ye have arrived there, will clothe yourselves with garments from off the wishing-trees."

title.en: Glooskap and Malsum, the Twin Brothers
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與狼弟馬爾蘇姆

region.en: Nova Scotia / Gaspe peninsula, Wabanaki country
region.zh: 瓦巴納基之地：新斯科舍／加斯佩半島

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of Glooskap's Birth, and of his Brother Malsum the Wolf'

summary.en: The good Glooskap and his evil twin Malsum the Wolf, who burst through their mother's side and killed her, exchange the secrets of their lives; the Wolf, betrayed and betrayed again, smites his brother with pine and owl-feather in vain — until a fern-root, learned from the Beaver, proves his bane.
summary.zh: 善神格魯斯卡普與惡弟狼馬爾蘇姆乃孿生；弟破母肋而出，弒其母。兄弟互換命門之秘：狼以松根、鴞羽擊兄而皆不驗——終自河貍處洩出「蕨根」之秘，格魯斯卡普一擊而斃之。

sensitivity.note: Wabanaki oral tradition recorded from named Indian narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Wabanaki/Algonquian communities.

passages.text: Now the great lord Glooskap, who was worshiped in after-days by all the Wabanaki, or children of light, was a twin with a brother. As he was good, this brother, whose name was Malsumsis, or Wolf the younger, was bad. Before they were born, the babes consulted to consider how they had best enter the world. And Glooskap said, "I will be born as others are." But the evil Malsumsis thought himself too great to be brought forth in such a manner, and declared that he would burst through his mother's side. And as they planned it so it came to pass. Glooskap as first came quietly to light, while Malsumsis kept his word, killing his mother.

It came to pass in after-days that Kwah-beet-a-sis, the son of the Great Beaver, or, as others say, Miko the Squirrel, or else the evil which was in himself, tempted Malsumsis to kill Glooskap; for in those days all men were wicked. So taking his bow he shot Ko-ko-khas the Owl, and with one of his feathers he struck Glooskap while sleeping. [...] Therefore Glooskap arose in sorrow and in anger, took a fern-root, sought Malsumsis in the deep, dark forest, and smote him so that he fell down dead.

title.en: Glooskap Makes Man of the Ash Tree
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普以梣樹造人

region.zh: 瓦巴納基之地：緬因／新斯科舍

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap made the Elves and Fairies, and then Man of an Ash Tree'

summary.en: Glooskap came first into the land next to sunrise: he shot his arrows into the basket-trees, the Ash, and the first Indians came out of the bark; then, finding the animals he had made too strong, he questioned Moose, Squirrel, and Bear, and made each smaller — or banished them — according to their answers.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普初至日出之地；彎弓射梣樹，樹皮中湧出最初之印第安人。又見所造之獸過強，乃問麋、松鼠、白熊：「遇人則何為？」聽其答而各縮其形，或逐之遠方。

sensitivity.note: Wabanaki oral tradition recorded from named Indian narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Wabanaki/Algonquian communities.

passages.text: Glooskap came first of all into this country, into Nova Scotia, Maine, Canada, into the land of the Wabanaki, next to sunrise. There were no Indians here then (only wild Indians very far to the west). First born were the Mikumwess, the Oonabgemessuk, the small Elves, little men, dwellers in rocks. And in this way he made Man: He took his bow and arrows and shot at trees, the basket-trees, the Ash. Then Indians came out of the bark of the Ash-trees. [...] Glooskap made all the animals. He made them at first very large. [...] Then he said to the Squirrel, who was of the size of a Wolf, "What would you do if you should meet an Indian?" And the Squirrel answered, "I would scratch down trees on him." Then Glooskap said, "You also are too strong," and he made him little. [...] So he questioned all the beasts, changing their size or allotting their lives according to their answers.

title.en: Sky Woman and the Good Mind, the Bad Mind

region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加之地

texts.period: Iroquois tradition as written by David Cusick (Tuscarora), 1827/1848; quoted in Leland, 1884

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations (1848), as quoted in Leland, Algonquin Legends of New England

summary.en: David Cusick's Iroquois account: a pregnant woman of the upper world descends and is received on the turtle; her twin sons, the Good Mind and the Bad Mind, break into the dark world — the Good makes the sun and moon of their mother's head and body, creates creeks, animals, and two breathing figures of dust, while the Bad raises mountains and falls to spite him.
summary.zh: 卡西克所記易洛魁神話：上界孕婦下墜，落於龜背；孿生二子善心與惡心破腹而出，入黑暗世界。善心以母之顱造日、以身造月，作川流動物，又以土塑男女二像吹以生氣；惡心則造高山飛瀑以相抗。

sensitivity.note: Iroquois tradition as written down by a Tuscarora author in 1827/1848; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Haudenosaunee communities.

passages.text: There was a woman who was with child, with twins. She descended from the higher world, and was received on the turtle. While she was in the distress of travail, one of the infants in her womb was moved by an evil desire, and determined to pass out under the side of the parent's arm, and the other infant endeavored in vain to prevent his design. They entered the dark world by compulsion, and their mother expired in a few minutes. One of them possessed a gentle disposition, and was named Enigorio, the Good Mind. The other possessed an insolence of character, and was called Enigonhahetgea; that is, the Bad Mind. [...] The Good Mind, determined to prosecute his design, began the work of creation. Of his mother's head he made the sun, of her body the moon. After he had made creeks and rivers, animals and fishes, he formed two images of the dust of the ground in his own likeness, male and female, and by his breathing into their nostrils he gave them living souls

title.en: The Children Throw the Sleeping Sun into the Sky

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Children are sent to throw the sleeping Sun into the Sky'

summary.en: The Sun lies sleeping with his armpit shining on the ground; an old woman sends the children to seize him together and throw him up into the sky, telling him to stand fast and travel hot — so the Sun became the Sun which dries the Bushman rice as he passes along above.
summary.zh: 太陽熟睡，腋下光芒照地；老嫗遣孩童共執而舉擲於天，囑其站定而行、熾熱如常——太陽遂為今日之太陽，行於天上，曝乾桑人之米。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: they waited for him (the Sun), they went to sit down. They arose, going on, they stealthily approached him, they stood still, they looked at him, they went forward; they stealthily reached him, they took hold of him, they all took hold of him together, lifted him up, they raised him, while he felt hot. Then, they threw him up, while he felt hot; they spoke to him, while he felt hot: "O Sun! thou must altogether stand fast, thou must go along, thou must stand fast, while thou art hot."

The old woman said to the children: "O children going yonder! ye must tell him, that, he must altogether become the Sun, that he may go forward, while he feels that he is altogether the Sun, which is hot; therefore, the Bushman rice becomes dry, while he is hot, passing along in the sky; he is hot, while he stands above in the sky."

title.en: The Moon and the Origin of Death

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Origin of Death'

summary.en: The Moon meant mankind to be like himself: dying, and then coming again living back; but the Hare contradicted him, declaring his mother utterly dead — and the Moon, enraged, struck his mouth and cursed the people to die altogether and vanish away, while the hare ever after bears the scar.
summary.zh: 月神本欲人類如己：死而復生；野兔逆其言，堅稱其母已真死。月神怒擊其口而咒人類：「爾等必盡死而滅」，兔唇之疤由此而來——死亡自此常駐人間。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: Therefore, the Moon spoke, he said: Ye who are people, ye shall, when ye die, altogether dying vanish away. For, I said, that, ye should, when ye died, ye should again arise, ye should not altogether die. For, I, when I am dead, I again living return. I had intended, that, ye who are men, ye should also resemble me [...] The hare, when I intended to tell him about it, -- while I felt that I knew that the hare's mother had not really died, for, she slept, -- the hare was the one who said to me, that his mother did not sleep; for, his mother had altogether died. These were the things that I became angry about

And the Moon became angry about it, that the hare spoke thus, while he did not assent to him (the Moon). And he hit with his fist, cleaving the hare's mouth; and while he hit the hare's mouth with his fist, he exclaimed: "This person, his mouth which is here, his mouth shall altogether be like this, even when he is a hare; he shall always bear a scar on his mouth..."

title.en: The Mantis Feigns Death as a Hartebeest

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Mantis assumes the form of a Hartebeest'

summary.en: |Kaggen the Mantis, the trickster of the early race, cheats the children by feigning death as a dead hartebeest; they joyfully skin him with stone knives — until his skin snatches itself free, and the dismembered flesh springs together again, joining itself piece by piece to the living Mantis.
summary.zh: 早期之民的詭計者——螳螂|卡根——化身死麋羚詐騙孩童；孩童歡然以石刀剝皮——皮忽自脫手而遁，碎肉相尋，節節復接，螳螂復活如初。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: The Mantis is one who cheated the children, by becoming a hartebeest, by resembling a dead hartebeest. He feigning death lay in front of the children, when the children went to seek gambroo [...] The children perceived him, when he had laid himself stretched out, while his horns were turned backwards. The children then said to each other: "It is a hartebeest that yonder lies; it is dead." The children jumped for joy (saying): "Our hartebeest! we shall eat great meat." They broke off stone knives by striking (one stone against another), they skinned the Mantis. The skin of the Mantis snatched itself quickly out of the children's hands.

Her sisters let fall the flesh of the Mantis. The flesh of the Mantis sprang together, it quickly joined itself to the lower part of the Mantis's back. The head of the Mantis quickly joined (itself) upon the top of the neck of the Mantis. [...] The shoulder blade of the Mantis ran forward, it joined itself on to the ribs of the Mantis.
